newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: U.S. envoy reassures Seoul on Korean crisis.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy reassures Seoul on Korean crisis.

text.p: U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Winston Lord reassured South Korea on Thursday that Washington was concerned over recent North Korean actions that have heightened tension on the peninsula.
Lord, who is assistant secretary of state for East Asia and Pacific affairs, is scheduled to begin talks with South Korean leaders on Friday.

"I will be reviewing recent developments to ensure the closest possible policy coordination between Seoul and Washington," he said in a statement after arriving. "The United States is concerned by recent North Korean actions."

Lord's arrival for a three-day visit coincided with a massive manhunt by thousands of troops in rugged east coast woodlands for North Korean agents suspected of strangling an elderly woman and shooting dead two South Korean men.

South Korean troops sealed off all roads leading into the Mount Odae area where the bodies of the villagers were found covered in grass and branches on Wednesday as thousands of southern soldiers continued to comb the area on Thursday.
"There have been no developments yet but our soldiers are still aggressively searching the area," a Defence Ministry official told Reuters.

Seoul suspects the villagers, last seen picking wild mushrooms in the area on Tuesday, were killed by three of 26 North Korean agents who came ashore from a grounded submarine last month about 70 km (44 miles) from Mount Odea.
Twenty-two of the northern agents were killed by Southern troops or found dead, while one has been captured.
The submarine incident has provoked angry threats from both Koreas, which remain divided by a fragile ceasefire since the end of the 1950-53 Korean War.
On Thursday, communist Pyongyang denied its agents had killed the villagers and accused Seoul of fabricating the case and pushing the peninsula to the brink of war.
In a communique carried by North Korea's official news agency, Pyongyang also denounced South Korea for failing to return the bodies of the dead North Koreans and the survivors along with the vessel.
"Facts show the South Korean rulers intend to expand the incident and drive the situation to the brink of war," the statement said.

Seoul has prodded the U.N. Security Council to take a tough stand against North Korean threats of "merciless retaliation" for the deaths of its agents while tightening security around the country amid warnings of terrorist action by Pyongyang.

On Thursday, South Korea's Capital Defence Command in charge of defending Seoul and surrounding areas said it would conduct an anti-espionage drill early on Friday, reinforcing an atmosphere of general alarm in the wake of Pyongyang's threats.

Pyongyang, in its statement on Thursday, repeated its threat to make South Korea "pay thousandfold in any time and any form for the blood shed" by its soldiers. "Time will prove how dearly they will have to pay," it added.

China, which backed the North in the Korean War and remains one of Pyongyang's few diplomatic allies, said on Thursday saying it was willing to cooperate with other countries to maintain peace on the Korean peninsula.

"China is willing to cooperate with other countries to bring into play positive and constructive action to uphold the peninsula's peace and stability," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told a briefing in Beijing.
